passage: Ranks? Okay, here's what I saw. I'm Jomon, Class 10, and it happened to my friend Harish. In term one our school pinned a rank list outside the staffroom every month. Harish was number four, Leena number five, me number six. Suddenly Harish stopped lending his physics notes. Leena started studying in the library corner where no one could see her pages. Nobody said anything mean. Everyone just went quiet about what they knew, like knowledge was something you could lose by showing it. In term two a new teacher put us in groups of four with one shared score for projects. First week, Harish was explaining vectors to Leena on the back bench, drawing arrows on her palm with a pen. Same people, same syllabus. Only the rules had changed, and the notes came out of the bags again.

qa.q: What rank was Harish on the term-one list?
qa.a: Harish was number four.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling as classmates went quiet about what they knew?
qa.a: Jomon felt uneasy and a little sad, watching friends turn into guarded rivals even though nobody was being mean.

qa.q: Why did the group projects change how Harish behaved?
qa.a: With one shared score, helping Leena also helped Harish, so explaining vectors made more sense than hiding notes.

qa.q: How might Harish have felt about keeping his physics notes to himself?
qa.a: Harish may have felt pressured and a little guilty, protecting a rank while losing the easy friendship of sharing.

grounding: Jomon observes how a monthly ranking made classmates hide notes while shared-score group work made them help each other.

passage: Didi, you remember the poem thing? Let me, Hansa, tell it properly this time. I read my monsoon poem in Kamal Sir's class, and from the back someone shouted, "Copied from the internet!" Everybody laughed. Sir laughed a little too, then just said, "Next." I wanted to sink into the floor. The next morning he called me into the corridor before assembly. He said, "Hansa, yesterday I let that go on, and I shouldn't have. I'm sorry. Your poem was yours." Then in class he didn't name anyone. He said, "Yesterday this room got something wrong, including me. If you doubt someone's work, come to me quietly. We don't laugh people out of speaking here." The back row went red and stared at their desks. And didi, last Friday I read again. Nobody laughed except at the funny line.

qa.q: What did someone shout when Hansa read the monsoon poem?
qa.a: Someone shouted, "Copied from the internet!"

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling right after the class laughed?
qa.a: Hansa felt humiliated and wanted to sink into the floor, made worse because Sir laughed a little too.

qa.q: Which of Kamal Sir's steps repaired things, and why?
qa.a: He apologised privately to Hansa first, then set the class norm without naming anyone, so nobody was shamed and trust came back.

qa.q: What might the back row have felt when Sir spoke to the class?
qa.a: They probably felt embarrassed and caught out, but not publicly shamed, which left them room to change.

grounding: Shows a teacher repairing a humiliating moment by speaking privately with Hansa and addressing the class norm without shaming anyone.

subtype: Speaking up in a large lecture [Actor]
passage:
Monday. In the two-hundred-seat hall, Professor Iyer raced through eigenvalues. Karthik's question sat in his throat: why does the matrix have to be square? He looked at the rows of nodding heads and wrote it in his margin instead, underlined twice. Beside him, Rehana was drawing tiny spirals.
Wednesday. The tutorial sheet was all square matrices, and Karthik was stuck on the first problem. In the canteen Rehana admitted she had copied the worked example without understanding a line. So had two others at their table.
Friday. Palms sweating, Karthik raised his arm halfway through the lecture. "Sorry, basic doubt: why must it be square?" A few heads turned. The professor smiled and spent five minutes on it. Afterwards, three strangers stopped him on the stairs. "Thanks, yaar. I've had that exact question since Monday."

qa.q: What was Karthik's question?
qa.a: Why the matrix has to be square.

qa.q: Why did Karthik write the question in his margin on Monday instead of asking it?
qa.a: He was afraid of looking ignorant in front of rows of nodding students, so embarrassment won over curiosity.

qa.q: What could Karthik remind himself before the next big lecture?
qa.a: If something confuses him, others are probably confused too, so asking early helps the whole hall, not just him.

qa.q: How did the three strangers on the stairs see Karthik's question?
qa.a: They were grateful and relieved, because they had carried the same doubt since Monday and hadn't dared to ask.

grounding: Shows a college student holding back a question in a big hall, then asking and finding others were grateful for it.

subtype: Training or class culture as a young teacher [Actor]
passage: I'm Simran, and my first lesson with Class 8 still makes me wince. I wanted so badly to be the fun teacher. Ten minutes in, Megha mixed up mass and weight, and Gautam called out, "Even my little brother knows that!" A few kids laughed. I laughed too, just a bit, to seem relaxed. Megha didn't speak again that day. Two days later Gautam interrupted again, and this time I had planned for it. "Gautam, hold that thought. Hand up next time." Calm, the same tone I'd use with anyone. When Asha, my quietest student, blurted an answer out of turn, I said exactly the same to her. It felt stiff and not very popular. By the third week hands were going up, and Megha asked me a question about gravity. Being liked would have been easier. Being fair made the room safe.

qa.q: What did Megha mix up in the first lesson?
qa.a: Megha mixed up mass and weight.

qa.q: Why did Simran laugh along at Gautam's remark in the first lesson?
qa.a: Simran was anxious to be liked as the fun teacher, and that wish won over protecting Megha; the memory still brings a wince of regret.

qa.q: What changed in Simran's approach, and why did it help?
qa.a: Simran planned one calm response to interruptions and used it for everyone, even Asha, so the class saw the rules were fair and safe.

qa.q: What was that first lesson like for Megha?
qa.a: Megha was laughed at for a mistake, even by the teacher, and went silent for the rest of the day.

grounding: Simran, a young teacher, learns that the response to the first mistake and first interruption sets the tone, and fairness matters more than being liked.

passage: Kamal's first real deadline arrived on his ninth day at the logistics firm: the vendor summary, due at five. At 4:40 he hit send, addressed to his manager, Ms Rao, alone. Within a minute Vishal, two desks over, leaned across. "You didn't copy Farooq sir?" "Is that a rule?" "Not written anywhere. But he handles the vendors, so he expects it." Kamal's neck went hot. He resent the mail with an apologetic line and then sat very still, replaying every email he had sent that week. In the 5:30 meeting he noticed that nobody spoke before Ms Rao did, and that Vishal waited for Farooq sir to finish before disagreeing. Kamal opened his notebook to a fresh page and wrote a title at the top: "Things no one says."

qa.q: When was the vendor summary due?
qa.a: It was due at five.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling after Vishal pointed out the missing name?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and anxious; his neck went hot and he replayed every email of the week, afraid of other missteps.

qa.q: What small step helped Kamal start learning the office's hidden rules?
qa.a: Watching the meeting closely and noting patterns on a "Things no one says" page, while asking a friendly colleague like Vishal when unsure.

qa.q: How might Vishal see Kamal's mistake?
qa.a: Vishal probably sees it as an ordinary new-joiner slip and wants to save Kamal trouble, not embarrass him.

grounding: Shows a new graduate discovering under deadline pressure that the office's real rules are unwritten, and watching anxiously to learn them.

passage: At the tehsil office in Hoshiarpur, Ankita's internship had become photocopying. Three weeks of it. On Thursday the head clerk, Mr Bedi, tossed a file onto her desk. "Two hundred copies. And don't stand there like a statue." The peon looked away. The other intern, Rupinder, kept his head down and hurried past. Ankita stapled until her thumb ached, wondering whether this was simply how offices worked or whether she was being punished for something. That evening she heard herself say, "I'll come early tomorrow, sir, anything you need," and hated how small her voice sounded. Jasleen, the junior officer who had signed her internship form, found her at the tea stall. "Copying is normal for interns," Jasleen said. "Being barked at is not. Keep a note of what you're asked to do. And on Monday, you're coming on my site visit."

qa.q: How many copies did Mr Bedi ask for?
qa.a: He asked for two hundred copies.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she offered to come early?
qa.a: She felt small and anxious to please, unsure whether she was being punished, and hated how her voice sounded.

qa.q: How did Jasleen help Ankita tell normal from unfair?
qa.a: Jasleen separated the two plainly, copying is normal but being barked at is not, and gave practical steps: note the tasks and join the site visit.

qa.q: What might Rupinder be going through as he keeps his head down?
qa.a: Rupinder may feel the same fear and choose silence to stay safe, which makes the sharp tone look normal to everyone.

grounding: Shows an intern given menial work and spoken to sharply, unsure what is normal, until a trusted mentor helps her tell the difference.

passage: Mehak, you think this only happens to you? Sit. When I was twenty-four, at the survey office in Pune, I built a whole new sampling plan, three weeks of late nights. At the review meeting my senior, Mr Khanna, stood up and presented it as "an idea I've been developing". Six people nodded. I sat there with my hands shaking under the table, so angry I couldn't taste my tea. I wanted to stand up and shout. My friend Leela pressed her foot on mine. Afterwards she said, "Shout today and you're the difficult girl for ten years." So I went home and wrote down dates, drafts, every email with my name on the file. On the next project I sent my plan to the whole team on day one. Nobody could borrow that one. That is how your Nirmala Aunty learnt, beta.

qa.q: How long had young Nirmala worked on the sampling plan?
qa.a: She spent three weeks of late nights building it.

qa.q: What was young Nirmala feeling when Mr Khanna presented her plan?
qa.a: She was angry and helpless, her hands shaking under the table, so upset she couldn't taste her tea.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Nirmala protected her work?
qa.a: Instead of shouting, she recorded dates, drafts and emails, and on the next project sent her plan to the whole team on day one.

qa.q: Why might Leela have pressed her foot on Nirmala's in the meeting?
qa.a: Leela was worried a public outburst would get her friend labelled difficult for years and wanted to protect her.

grounding: Nirmala Aunty recalls a senior presenting her work as his, and learning that documenting and sharing early is safer than a public confrontation.

passage: Jeevan had worked out the Gurugram office within a month: lunch with the right people, a joke in the regional head's chat, a coffee order remembered. None of it felt wrong. It was just how you got noticed. The trouble started with the client pitch. Deepak had found the costing error that saved it, and at the Friday review everyone turned to him. That night Jeevan drafted a message to the regional head: "Deepak's numbers were a bit shaky earlier, I helped tighten them." It wasn't quite a lie. His thumb hovered over send. He thought of Deepak, who had lent him a charger on his first day, and of Nisha from HR saying, "People here remember who stood on whom." He deleted the second line. Then, slowly, the first.

qa.q: What had Deepak found that saved the client pitch?
qa.a: Deepak had found the costing error that saved it.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as his thumb hovered over send?
qa.a: He was torn and uneasy: ambition pushed him to grab credit, but remembering Deepak's kindness made him hesitate.

qa.q: Where does Jeevan's networking cross a line, and what is fine to keep?
qa.a: Lunches and remembering people's orders are normal; the drafted message undermines Deepak with a half-truth, so deleting it was right.

qa.q: What would change for Deepak if the message had been sent?
qa.a: The regional head might quietly doubt Deepak's work without Deepak ever knowing why, hurting a colleague who had been kind.

grounding: Shows an ambitious employee whose normal networking nearly turns into undermining a colleague, and who pulls back.

passage:
Dear Preeti,
When I left college you told me to stay out of office wars. I'm trying. It's harder than you made it sound.
Our design team has split in two since the new head arrived. Aslam's side wants the old process; Karan's side wants the new tool. I told both I'd work with whatever we decide. Now Aslam's people stop talking when I walk into the pantry, and Karan copied me on an email "for my support" that I never gave.
Last week, when the release slipped, both camps pointed at my module. Nobody defended it. I felt proud of staying fair, and completely alone.
I'm not going to pick a side. But I think I need two or three people who know my work and will say so quietly. Is that politics, or just sense?
Write when you can,
Pankaj

qa.q: What did Karan do that Pankaj never agreed to?
qa.a: Karan copied Pankaj on an email "for my support" that Pankaj never gave.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when both camps blamed the module?
qa.a: Pankaj felt proud of staying fair but also completely alone, because nobody defended the work.

qa.q: What would you advise Pankaj about finding allies?
qa.a: Build quiet trust with a few colleagues who see the work directly and can vouch for its quality, without joining either camp.

qa.q: How might Aslam's side see Pankaj's neutrality?
qa.a: They may read it as secretly siding with Karan, especially after that email, which is why they fall silent in the pantry.

grounding: Pankaj's email shows an employee staying out of rival camps, getting pressed by both, and seeing the need for quiet allies.

passage: On his first Monday at the architecture studio in Hamburg, Siddiq noticed the lights. At nine at night every desk was still lit. Emil, who had been there two years, was eating cold pasta over his keyboard. When the director walked past, the room went quiet, and Emil straightened like a schoolboy. At Tuesday's meeting a late drawing was blamed on "someone in the team"; nobody asked who, and three people stared at their laptops. "It's just how it is here," Emil told him at the coffee machine, smiling in a tired way. That night Siddiq typed a note on his phone: "Week one: fear, late hours, blame. Why does no one blink?" Then he added a line: "Read this again in six months."

qa.q: What was Emil eating at nine at night?
qa.a: Emil was eating cold pasta over his keyboard.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq add "Read this again in six months" to the note?
qa.a: He was uneasy and worried that he too might stop noticing the fear and blame once they started to feel ordinary.

qa.q: What could Siddiq do to keep his fresh view without being swept along?
qa.a: He could keep writing down what he sees, talk with someone outside the studio, and set his own limits on late hours before they become habit.

qa.q: How does Emil seem to see the studio's culture?
qa.a: To Emil it has become normal; the tired smile and "just how it is" suggest he has stopped expecting anything different.

grounding: Siddiq, a newcomer, sees long hours, fear of the director and blame as strange while a longer-serving colleague treats them as ordinary.
